content: A total of 100 patients undergoing hip replacement surgery were randomized in the study, and all patients received treatment. The study population consisted of 45% men and 55% women. After achieving hemostasis, treatment was initiated 12 to 24 hours post-surgery and continued for 10 to 14 days. In a double-blind, multicenter study, three dosing regimens of Lovenox were compared in patients undergoing hip replacement surgery. A total of 572 patients were randomized, and 568 patients received treatment. The study population had a mean age of 67 years, with 63% men and 37% women. The racial distribution was 93% Caucasian, 6% Black, less than 1% Asian, and 1% other. Treatment was initiated within two days post-surgery and continued for 7 to 11 days. No significant difference in efficacy was observed between the 30 mg every 12 hours regimen and the 40 mg once-daily regimen. In another double-blind study, Lovenox 30 mg every 12 hours subcutaneously was compared to placebo in patients undergoing knee replacement surgery. A total of 132 patients were randomized, and 131 patients received treatment. Of these, 99 underwent total knee replacement, while 32 underwent either unicompartmental knee replacement or tibial osteotomy. The study population included 44% men and 56% women. After hemostasis was achieved, treatment was initiated 12 to 24 hours post-surgery and continued for up to 15 days. The incidence of proximal and total deep vein thrombosis (DVT) was significantly lower in the Lovenox group compared to the placebo group. In an open-label, parallel-group, randomized clinical study, Lovenox 30 mg every 12 hours subcutaneously was compared to heparin 5000 units every 8 hours subcutaneously in patients undergoing elective knee replacement surgery. A total of 453 patients were randomized, and all received treatment. The study population had a mean age of 68 years, with 41% men and 59% women. Treatment was initiated post-surgery and continued for up to 14 days. The incidence of deep vein thrombosis was significantly lower in the Lovenox group compared to the heparin group. In a study of extended prophylaxis for patients undergoing hip replacement surgery, patients were treated with Lovenox 40 mg subcutaneously while hospitalized, starting up to 12 hours prior to surgery for the prevention of postoperative DVT. At the end of the perioperative period, all patients underwent bilateral venography. In a double-blind design, patients without venous thromboembolic disease were randomized to a post-discharge regimen of either Lovenox 40 mg once daily subcutaneously (n = 90) or placebo (n = 89) for three weeks. A total of 179 patients were randomized in the double-blind phase, and all received treatment. The study population had a mean age of 64 years, with 57% men and 43% women. The incidence of DVT during extended prophylaxis was significantly lower in the Lovenox group compared to the placebo group. In a second study, patients undergoing hip replacement surgery were treated with Lovenox 40 mg subcutaneously while hospitalized, starting up to 12 hours prior to surgery. All patients were examined for clinical signs and symptoms of venous thromboembolic (VTE) disease. In a double-blind design, patients without clinical signs and symptoms of VTE disease were randomized to a post-discharge regimen of either Lovenox 40 mg once daily subcutaneously (n = 131) or placebo (n = 131) for three weeks.
